  registered workspace listings (current or any other) without binding the

  duplicates.

  only in memory, and refresh on every accepted message.

fix(qq): stop flashing the status frame during tool runs

The shared Harness client emits a '正在整理结果…' status update after
every tool/result. Pushing each one into the QQ stream message made
multi-tool turns repeatedly flash that notice instead of showing real
progress. Skip status frames in the QQ onUpdate handler so the stream
keeps the last meaningful frame (tool name or generated text), which
matches the official dsh-qqbot behaviour of not pushing tool-noise.

feat(qq): push progress and answers as separate messages

Replace the in-place streaming reply (openStream replace-mode frames)
with discrete pushed messages, so the chat no longer flickers while
the turn is running:

- each tool call pushes one notice message (正在使用X…); status frames
  such as '正在整理结果…' and per-token text frames are not pushed
- the final answer arrives as one new markdown message
- a stopped turn still announces '已停止。'; no stream session is
  created, so there is nothing to cancel or finalize

feat(qq): stream the full turn feed as discrete messages

Show what the agent is actually doing during a turn, the way Claude
Code does: interim explanation text, every Tool call, and the error
detail when a tool fails, each as its own pushed message before the
final markdown answer.

- HarnessReplyTracker.consume now returns every frame of a polling
  batch in order (same-batch text frames collapse to the latest)
  instead of dropping all but the last event, which silently ate
  tool-call frames that shared a batch with their result
- tool frames carry callId; status frames carry the correlated
  toolName and a flattened error text parsed from the tool/result
  error payload (message, or name: code)
- the QQ bridge holds interim step text until the next tool call
  (or the end of the turn) pushes it, emits 'Tool call <name>' per
  call, emits 'Tool call <name>\nError: <reason>' for failures, and
  skips re-sending interim text that already equals the final answer

Other channels keep their existing behaviour: the status frame still

fix(feishu): honor NO_PROXY before proxying the long connection

webSocketProxyUrl() picks up https_proxy/HTTPS_PROXY/http_proxy/
HTTP_PROXY and forces the Feishu WSS long connection through the proxy,
without consulting NO_PROXY/no_proxy. With a local proxy exported in

in a loop, so the bot never reaches a stable connected state.

(open.feishu.cn / open.larksuite.com) before falling back to the proxy
env: exact host, parent-domain (.cn, feishu.cn) and * entries follow
the common NO_PROXY semantics.

fix(dingtalk): stop AI Card from going blank at finish

Three real bugs in the DingTalk AI Card lifecycle left the card blank
or showing a generic close-out message instead of the model's answer:

- createAiCard built the card in three separate requests (create with
  an empty cardData, deliver, then a follow-up PUT to fill it). The
  chat showed an empty card shell for the gap between deliver and the
  fill PUT, and stayed blank forever if that PUT ever failed. It now
  uses POST /v1.0/card/instances/createAndDeliver with the thinking
  text already in cardData, matching DingTalk's documented pattern.

- cardData() always left staticMsgContent empty and pinned
  sys_full_json_obj.order to msgContent. The AI Card template renders
  msgContent while streaming (flowStatus '2') but switches to
  staticMsgContent once the streaming widget tears down, so a
  finished or failed card rendered blank even though the answer had
  streamed correctly moments earlier. staticMsgContent now mirrors
  msgContent and the order key switches with flowStatus.

- finishAiCard wrote the final answer into the last streaming frame
  (isFinalize: true) and then issued a second PUT /v1.0/card/instances
  with the same content, retried once on failure. That second request
  raced the template's streaming teardown and could wipe out the
  answer that the first request had just written. finishAiCard now
  makes only the one streaming request DingTalk's docs describe as
  the finish step.

- dingtalk-bridge.mjs sent a second webhook text reply whenever
  cardStream.finish() returned false, even though the card had
  already been shown to the user. That produced a blank/stale card
  sitting next to a duplicate plain-text reply. Once a card has
  started, the bridge now never falls back to a second text message;
  it logs the failure and leaves the delivered card as the single
  reply.

with a synced DM target are now rendered through the bridge's own
target openId, sendCard branched to open_id delivery), so they get the
identical process-card ladder as IM turns — panels, chunk spillover,

- mid-turn adoption: if the bridge starts while a turn is running, the
  first visible event adopts it so the mirror still renders.
- turn/end seals the card and clears the target.
- Remove the parallel SessionSyncRenderer and its wiring (coordinator

* fix(feishu): adopt opens the mirror card; add delivery diagnostics

Mid-turn adoption now opens the #stepCards mirror card immediately
(before the adopt-fix the card was never created, so every event
re-resolved targets and nothing rendered). Delivery diagnostics
(console.error) added at the open_id sendCard branch and proactive text
entry to locate a 230001 invalid receive_id seen in live testing.

* fix(feishu): restore sessionSyncTargetsFor constructor wiring lost in rebase

* fix(feishu): widen event entry so the session-sync mirror sees every type

the session-sync mirror branch could run, so turn/start never opened
the mirror card and tool/assistant events never fed it — the mirror
could only ever see turn/end (with no card to seal). The entry now
admits all sequenced events; non-turn/end events return after the
mirror branch, preserving the original watch-completion behavior for
turn/end.

* fix(feishu): skip mirror turns via interaction ownership; log mirror failures

The #stepCards probe raced the first process update (the mirror opened
for IM turns before their own card existed). The session-sync branch
now consults hasActiveHarnessInteractionOwner, which the bridge's own
ask registers before the turn starts. Mirror-card render failures are
surfaced at error level so delivery problems are visible in journals.

* fix(feishu): identify IM turns via in-flight ask keys, not the interaction registry

hasActiveHarnessInteractionOwner reads the interaction-card ownership
table, which IM asks without buttons never populate — so mirror cards
double-rendered for plain IM turns. The bridge now records each
in-flight conversation key in #imTurnKeys before calling ask and clears
it in markAskComplete; the mirror branch resolves the key->session
mapping, which is authoritative at turn/start time.

* fix(feishu): guard mid-turn adoption against IM turns too

The turn/start skip worked, but the next tool event then hit the
mid-turn adoption branch, which had no IM check, and opened the mirror
anyway. Both paths now consult the same #isImTurn helper.

* feat(feishu): mirror Web/CLI sessions as process cards in synced DMs

Session-sync delivery targets so far mirrored conversations started
outside the IM (DSH Web / CLI) as a single plain text after the turn
finished. This renders them with the same process-card ladder as IM
turns: one live card patched in place, tool/thinking panels, byte-
budgeted chunk spillover, sealed terminal state, and the answer-
integrity invariant (post fallback only when the delivered render does
not cover the final answer).

The bridge consumes every Harness session event for sessions bound to
a synced DM target (host-resolved via the workspace store) and feeds
them through the regular #stepCards machine under a session-sync key,
with open_id delivery branched in #sendCard. IM-opened turns are
identified by their in-flight ask key and skipped, so they keep their
own card and are never double-rendered; mid-turn bridge restarts adopt
the running turn on its first visible event.

- #onHarnessEvent admits all sequenced events and routes them to
  #feedSessionSyncTurn; non-turn/end events stop there.
- runtime/production wire a sessionSyncTargetsFor resolver that maps a
  session to its synced DM openIds, owned by the matching bot only.

* fix(feishu): suppress plain-text session sync while the mirror owns a turn

With the process-card mirror live, the plain-text coordinator delivered
the same turn twice (card + '[DSH 助手]' text). A module-level registry
(session-sync-registry) now carries one claim per session: the mirror
claims on card open (turn/start and mid-turn adoption) and releases at
turn/end; the coordinator checks the claim before its user echo and
final-answer deliveries and skips when the mirror holds the turn.

* fix(feishu): seal orphaned mirror cards after a restart

A restart kills the turn without a turn/end event, so the mirror card
on Feishu stayed 'running' forever. The mirror card's identity is now
persisted in the session state (mirrors: sessionId -> chatId + cardIds,
updated on first render and on chunk spill); at startup the bridge
re-seals every orphaned card with a 'stopped' status and clears the
entry.

* fix(feishu): carry the user's question inside the mirrored card

Suppressing the coordinator's plain-text user echo also removed the
only record of what the Web/CLI user asked. The mirror now opens its
card with a quoted question block (user/message, surfaceOp append),
keeping the DM self-contained while the card remains the single
delivery for the turn.

* fix(feishu): orphan seal keeps the card's last delivered content

The startup recovery re-patched orphan cards with an empty stopped
card, wiping their panels. setMirror now records the last delivered
card JSON (updated on first render and every chunk spill); the orphan
seal re-patches that JSON with only the status line swapped to
已停止 (stepStatusText exported for the bridge).

* fix(feishu): align mirror draft semantics with ask callbacks; label the echo

Mirror turns now keep a per-session pending step: the latest interim
assistant text streams as the answer draft and folds into the thinking
panel when a tool call proves it interim (morphStepCardAnswerToNote),
matching the ask-callback path instead of letting later drafts
overwrite earlier interim content. The quoted user echo gains an
explicit '我问' label so the question block is self-describing.

* fix(feishu): orphan recovery only claims stale mirror entries

A restart lands while a healthy turn may still be streaming; sealing
that card wiped its content down to a bare stopped line. Mirror entries
now carry claimedAt, and startup recovery only re-seals entries older
than ten minutes — anything fresher is left for its turn to finish.

* fix(feishu): unwrap the double-encoded mirror snapshot in orphan recovery

setMirror stores the card JSON via JSON.stringify of an already-encoded
string, so orphan recovery parsed only one layer, saw no body.elements,
and fell through to the empty stopped card that wiped the mirror.
Unwrap until the card object appears.

* fix(feishu): clear the mirror entry after the seal, not before

The render chain trailing inside finishStepCard re-writes the mirror
entry (lastContent/cardIds) after an earlier clear, leaving a stale
running-state entry behind. Clear the entry after the seal completes.

* chore(feishu): drop the mirror delivery verification log

* fix(feishu): keep claimedAt across render updates; delay orphan recovery

Render-time setMirror overwrote the whole mirror entry, dropping
claimedAt so the age threshold never tripped and startup recovery
sealed live turns minutes old. Render updates now preserve the
original claim time, and recovery waits 90s after boot so in-flight
turns can re-adopt and finish before anything is judged orphaned.

* fix(feishu): seal mirrored cards on an event idle gap

The session-event mux forwards surfaced events (user/tool/assistant)
but not turn/start or turn/end, so a mirror card could never observe
the turn boundary and stayed 'running' forever. Arm an idle timer on
every mirrored event instead: 90s without a new event means the turn
has ended, so the card seals as completed with its current content and
the mirror entry clears. In-flight render chains are awaited first.

* fix(feishu): orphan threshold counts from last render activity

claimedAt is now a last-active timestamp refreshed by every successful
render, so a long-running healthy turn never looks orphaned, and the
recovery threshold shrinks to three minutes of silence.

* fix(feishu): address review findings on mirror integrity and scoping

Five issues from the maintainer review, each with a regression test:

1. Plain IM cards no longer write session-sync mirror state —
   persistMirrorState skips cards without a sessionSyncSessionId, so a
   restart can never wipe finished IM cards through the recovery.
2. A broken mirror no longer swallows the turn boundary: turn/end still
   releases the claim and clears the state on a broken card, and the
   first render failure releases the claim immediately so the plain-text
   coordinator takes over delivery (its user echo stays enabled to keep
   recipients established for the final-answer fallback).
3. Mirror claims are scoped per delivery target: the coordinator filters
   mirrored targets out of its final-answer delivery per target, so other
   synced targets (same or other channels) keep receiving text.
4. Plain IM replies (stepPush off) register their in-flight turn via
   beginImTurn in #answerWithStream, so the mirror never adopts them.
5. StateStore initializes the mirrors field for fresh stores — setMirror
   no longer throws TypeError on the first run.
6. setMirror stores stepStreamCard's raw JSON string (no double
   encoding), and orphan recovery leaves already-sealed chunks untouched.

callback_data limit, and every shape a keyboard cannot express — a refused
keyboard, multi-select, more than eight options, an unusable label — falls
back to the text flow the channel already had, numbered list included.

Also stop claiming user-questions/request exclusively in the host adapter.
It raced nothing, which kept the question out of DSH Web entirely and left
that surface with a card it could not answer. Race the host's own answerers

wrong thing:

  acknowledgement round-trip left a window and the guard only covered the
  final submission. The second press landed on the next question and wrote
  the first card's label into it as free text. Claim synchronously before
  the first await and refuse duplicates while a submission is in flight.
- A keyboard survived a text answer, and a later question restarts its
  indexes at zero, so an old card's buttons matched the new question. Carry
  a per-presentation nonce in callback_data and retire the keyboard when the
  text path answers too.
- The host answerer race swallowed every error, not just NO_PROVIDER,
  turning real failures into a hang. Log anything else.

fix(outbound): stage artifacts with the turn observed on the session event stream

and exposes neither an events array nor snapshotEvents(), so
currentTurn() resolves null during a real agent turn even while the
plugin's own session/event subscription already tracks the open turn in
#openTurns. OutboundArtifactRegistry.stage() consulted only
currentTurn(), so dsh_im_return_file always threw

fix(host): scope question retirement to the question itself

`dsh-agent-loop` mints one abort controller per turn and every tool call in that
turn shares the one signal. Under PTC the program waiting on this answer
subscribes to that signal by EVENT rather than by reading `signal.aborted`:

(dsh-code-runtime-worker-thread `onAbort`). Dispatching `abort` on it after an

answered once on IM, failed with `code run failed (abort)`.

Each question now owns a private AbortController: real upstream cancellation is
forwarded into it, and it is handed downstream as `request.signal`, so every
listener on the waterfall (the Remote/Web forwarder that renders the card, and
the IM pending) shares a lifetime that ends with this question instead of with
the turn. IM winning ends that lifetime; a host answer still leaves it alone.

fix(im): pair injected context with the user message it described

Context enhancement wrote its `<dsh_im_source>` and `<dsh_im_source_guidance>` blocks into the user prompt text, so the transcript showed raw tags inside the user's own message and the durable log could not tell plugin-added content from what the person typed. The prompt RPC carries no message source, so those blocks cannot travel as structured data.

Split them back out on the Host at `agent/pre-step` — the one point where the messages admitted to a step are already claimed and nothing is committed yet. The channel-side prefix is unchanged: a new rewriter parses it strictly, returns the user message with only its own text (keeping its id and source), and adds up to two plugin-sourced context messages beside it. Pairing follows message identity, never inbox position, so pre-staging context through `agent.inject()` is avoided: a step claims all of `next-step` plus exactly one `next-turn`, which would hand every context to the first prompt and leave later ones unattributed.

A prefix that does not match the producer grammar, a rejected step, or a rewrite error leaves the decision untouched, so the inline prefix remains the fallback; a Host without the Agent loop never dispatches the event. No bridge call site changes and the channel behavior baseline is preserved.

Add 14 regression tests covering the producer/parser round trip, tag-constant drift, non-prefix text, per-message pairing across a batch, identity preservation, empty-content safety, and the installer's reject, throw, and no-context paths. Record the mechanism and its boundaries in docs/方案. Validated 2769 tests on Node 24.21.0 with no failures, cancellations or skips; host/client build and package verification passed.

The `<dsh_im_reply_to>` block was the last injected block still written into the user prompt text, so the transcript showed the raw tag and its JSON payload inside the user's own bubble — up to 8000 characters of quoted text that could not be collapsed. Extend the `agent/pre-step` splitter that already carries the source block and guidance to recognise the reply block as well.

Blocks may now occupy several leading text parts, because a channel writes its source prefix as one part and the quoted reply as another, so the scan advances part by part instead of inspecting only the first. The reply row precedes the user message while the source and guidance rows follow it: the quoted material is what the person pointed at, so quoted-then-asked keeps the reading order, and the source describes the message that follows it. The reply row is labelled 引用/Quoted from the mirrored Host interface language, with the author appended when the reference names one.

The reply producer now shares the injected tag literals with the splitter, so the encoding and its parser cannot drift. Invalid JSON, a rejected step, or a rewrite error still leaves the decision untouched and the blocks inline.

Add 4 regression tests for reply parsing, the label fallback, reply-shaped non-JSON text, and the [reply, user, source] ordering; the existing suite covers the generalised multi-part scan. Record both block families in docs/方案. Validated 2773 tests on Node 24.21.0 with no failures, cancellations or skips; host/client build and package verification passed.

feat(im): carry source guidance as session prompt context

Context enhancement repeated the operator's guidance in every user message, so a long conversation accumulated one identical `dsh-im` row per turn. Guidance is not per-message data but per-conversation policy, so it now travels the Host's own channel for that: a channel publishes the guidance it composed when it dispatches the prompt, and the Host materializes it as dynamic prompt context — one durable snapshot per Session, re-rendered only when the published text changes.

Recording it needs the session identity at assembly time, which the prompt RPC does not carry, so a module-level registry (the shape `outboundArtifactRegistry` already uses) is filled by `HarnessClient.ask()` from the blocks it is about to send and read by a `systemPrompt.context` provider gated on that service through `ctx.inject`. Because this is the Host's own mechanism, its two consequences are accepted rather than worked around: the text is a prompt template whose unknown `{{name}}` references fail the step, and a deployment that suppresses dynamic runtime context omits the guidance.

The message-side copy is kept until a session's published guidance matches the block, so a prompt that never reached the registry — a pending message restored after a restart, for instance — still delivers its guidance, and nothing is lost if the context provider never registers.

Add 5 regression tests for guidance extraction from a composed prompt, suppression of an already-materialized body, the registry's publish/clear/forget paths, the provider's per-session value plus `agent/disposed` release, and the `ctx.inject(['systemPrompt'])` gate. fix(im): give a mid-turn correction its own source block

`/steer` sent the bare instruction, so the model could not tell which group member corrected the running task — the one place where attribution matters most, because a correction outranks the message that opened the turn. The command path now composes the same `<dsh_im_source>` block an ordinary message gets, captured when the command runs and filled with whoever issued the correction rather than the sender of the opening message.

Composing a string keeps both delivery paths untouched: `steerActiveTurn` still receives text, and the in-process control executor still builds its `agent.inject` message from that text. The existing `agent/pre-step` splitter then records the block as its own context row, exactly as it does for a prompt.

Every command entry point supplies the provenance: the shared fast-command path used by five channels, the WeCom family's own paths, DingTalk's message and menu paths, QQ's message and menu paths, and Feishu's message path plus its two card paths, which use the operator identity and recover the topic id from the conversation key because card routes do not carry the raw event.

Add 3 regression tests for the composed steering text, the unchanged bare instruction, and a disabled scope producing no enhancement. Validated 2781 tests on Node 24.21.0 with no failures, cancellations or skips; host/client build and package verification passed.

fix(im): keep user text out of guidance and split every valid source block

`HarnessClient.ask()` derived a Session's guidance by parsing the composed
prompt, so any user message whose text began with a `<dsh_im_source_guidance>`
block became that Session's configuration. This did not depend on the
enhancement switch, and a real source block in front of it changed nothing.
With an unregistered `{{variable}}` in the body the step failed outright,
because the Host renders dynamic context (`renderContextSections`) before it
dispatches `agent/pre-step`, so the splitter could never catch it; with a
plain-text body it silently entered the Session's prompt-context section, which
is a higher-trust channel than the user message the same text arrived in.

The value now travels out of band: a channel passes the guidance its captured
settings applied (`askInWorkspaceSession` -> `options.sourceGuidance`) and the

`guidanceInPromptContent` is deleted, so no code path can turn prompt text back

returning null made `blockAt()` treat the whole block as user text. That
disabled splitting for the message -- the quoted reply in it lost its row too,
and the guidance was not extracted either, so those configurations fell back to
the previous inline behavior. Whether a block is ours and whether it can
describe itself are now decided separately: a non-empty object drawn from the

Host-supplied `来源`/`Source` label. The claim rule is also stricter than
before, so unrelated JSON in user text is no longer mistaken for a source block.

Add a 255-subset round-trip test over the source-field selections, an adapter

guidance does, a per-channel test that all nine channels carry their captured
guidance, and a Host-label test for nameless rows. Validated 2817 tests on Node
24.21.0 with no failures, cancellations or skips; host/client build and package

* feat(email): add an IMAP/SMTP mailbox channel

Adds a two-way Email channel: mail sent to a dedicated mailbox is treated
as an instruction, and the Harness reply is delivered back inside the same
mail thread.

- email-api: IMAP polling, SMTP reply, and MIME parsing; quoted reply
  history is stripped so a thread does not grow the prompt every turn
- email-runtime: normalizes mail into the shared bridge message shape and
  maps Message-ID/References onto Harness conversations, so a reply joins
  the session that produced it
- email-controller: binds a mailbox (address + app password), verifying
  IMAP before persisting, and manages hosts, ports, and the allowlist
- config/state stores: provider presets plus a bounded Message-ID to
  conversation map
- The sender allowlist is required: a mail address is forgeable, so the
  channel fails closed rather than letting anyone drive the Harness
- Registered in the host channel list, the delivery adapter, and the
  client settings UI with Chinese and English text

The channel reuses TextHarnessBridge, so batching, approvals,
interactions, deferred delivery, and file return come for free.

* fix(email): register the channel through the shared startup path

The channel mounted its RPC only after production finished, so a failed
initialization left the settings page unreachable with a 404. It now uses
installProductionChannel, which mounts the endpoint first and swaps in the
real handler once ready.

Also fixes the failures that surfaced once the route existed:

- production was hand-rolled from the wecom-app assembly; it now delegates
  to createTokenProductionController (186 lines to 30) so the workspace
  scope, delivery adapter, and supervisor stay in one place
- the controller exposed bindMailbox only, while the shared token RPC
  handler requires bindCredentials; the mailbox method is now also exposed
  under that name
- the controller/runtime credential parameter is named token, matching the
  shared factory contract
- email and imessage were missing from the startup guidance tables, which
  rendered 'undefined初始化失败'; both are now named
- the invalid-config message list did not recognise 'Email', so a corrupt
  config.json reported a generic failure instead of the specific guidance

Verified against the running Host: the endpoint registers, connection.status
returns a healthy empty bot list, binding rejects a bad mailbox with the
localized error, and both the empty-allowlist and malformed-address guards
fail closed.

* fix(email): pass the channel's RPC call to the settings tab

The render site lists one RPC prop per channel by hand and email was
missing from that list, so the tab mounted without a call and rendered
'无法读取 Email 机器人状态 / Email 设置页缺少 RPC 连接'.

A guard test now derives the channel ids from the tab list and asserts the
settings inject block provides a matching RPC prop, so the next channel
cannot ship with the same gap. Verified by removing the prop: the guard
fails, and it passes once restored.

* fix(email): forward the mailbox form payload to the bind RPC

credentialPayload was () => ({}), which discarded every field the form
collected. The Host therefore received no address and rejected a valid
mailbox with '邮箱地址格式不正确'.

The values now pass through unchanged, so the Host sees the address, app
password, provider, and allowlist. A regression test asserts the payload
identity; reverting the fix makes it fail.

* fix(email): derive transport security from the port

Port 587 was treated as implicit TLS, which makes a STARTTLS submission
server hang instead of negotiating. The security mode is now derived the
way mail clients do it: 465 implicit TLS, 587/25/2525 STARTTLS with
requireTLS, everything else plain, and an explicit flag still wins. IMAP
follows the same rule with 993 as implicit TLS.

Verified against a real QQ mailbox: IMAP connects on 993 and SMTP submits
on 587.

* fix(email): read the mailbox secret from the credential wrapper

credentials.resolve() returns a wrapper whose payload lives on .value, the
same contract the shared token controller uses. Parsing the wrapper itself
threw and the error was swallowed by the catch, so a bound mailbox reported
configured: 1 but never started its runtime — no error, no log.

The secret is now unwrapped from .value before JSON.parse, the backup path
stores the plain value, and a regression test asserts a mailbox runtime
starts when the provider returns a wrapper.

* fix(email): use the shared attachment field names in both directions

Two field-name mismatches meant attachments never carried data:

- Outbound artifacts are materialized as { fileName, mediaType, bytes },
  but sendFile/sendImage read { name, content }, so every outgoing file
  was sent unnamed and empty. They now consume the shared shape.
- Inbound attachments declared `mimeType`, while the shared inbound-file
  layer reads `mediaType` — the type was silently dropped.

Both directions are covered by tests that fail when the wrong field is
restored.

* fix(email): filter by sender before downloading message bodies

A monitored mailbox also carries ordinary personal mail. The sender
allowlist was enforced inside the bridge, which runs after every body and
attachment had already been fetched and parsed, so unrelated mail was read
into the process even though it was never acted on.

Polling now reads envelopes first and checks the allowlist there; only
accepted senders have their source fetched. The two passes also avoid
nesting a fetch inside an active fetch iteration, which ImapFlow does not
support and which stalled the poll.

First connect additionally starts a short window below the mailbox tip, so
mail that arrives while the channel is starting is not skipped.

* fix(email): keep the mailbox allowlist and the access policy in sync

The sender allowlist lived in two stores: the mailbox config and the
Harness access policy. Only the config was updated, so after any allowlist
change the policy kept the original senders and the channel rejected every
new address — the message was received, marked seen, then silently dropped
because the policy no longer matched.

The derived policy is now pushed to the workspace store whenever the
allowlist changes, which is the store the runtime reads. The shared token
factory gains an opt-in hook for this so no other channel is affected.

* feat(email): session binding, subject headers, and recipient context

Three additions to the mailbox channel:

- Session binding with three levels of freedom, highest first: a per-sender
  pin, an account-wide pin, or no pin (each mail thread starts its own

  A bound conversation key resolves straight to the pinned session — without

  appear to save while having no effect.
- The subject and the To/Cc lists are prepended to the text the model sees.
  Previously only the body was forwarded, so an instruction written in the
  subject was silently dropped.
- The shared conversation store gains an opt-in extension hook so a channel
  can persist its own keys; the other channels are unaffected.

* fix(email): thread the RPC bridge to the account card and unwrap it

The session binding panel referenced rpcCall where it was not in scope, so
the whole IM settings slot crashed with a ReferenceError and rendered
nothing. The bridge and the reload callback are now passed down from the
settings tab that owns them.

The card receives the raw RPC bridge, whose response wraps the payload in
{ ok, value }; the panel treats it as the unwrapped value, so the sender
rows and the session list came back empty. It now unwraps and surfaces a
failed response as an error.

* i18n(email): add the missing English projection for the RPC error

* test(email): guard the account card's prop wiring

The settings tab owns the RPC bridge and threads it into each account
card. A missing prop there threw at render time and blanked the whole IM
settings slot, but the panel test passed the props in directly and so
never exercised the wiring.

The guard now derives the props the card reads from its own signature and
requires the render site to supply them all. Removing either rpcCall or
reload makes it fail; restoring them makes it pass.

* fix(email): keep the mailbox fields in the client snapshot

The shared snapshot normalizer keeps an explicit field list, so the
channel-specific mailbox fields were dropped on the way to the settings
form — the allowlist textarea rendered empty even though the Host was
returning the senders. The channel now declares them through the
normalizer's extension hook.

Also adds a 'point every sender at the same session' action, since several
senders frequently belong to one conversation.

* feat(email): allow the mailbox as its own sender, break the loop by RFC 3834

Rejecting every mail whose sender was the mailbox itself also blocked the
normal case of writing to the bot mailbox from that same mailbox to drive
the Harness.

Outgoing mail is now marked 'Auto-Submitted: auto-replied' (RFC 3834) and
incoming automatic replies are refused, so the channel can be its own
sender without two bots echoing each other. A sender written by hand still
runs, and 'Auto-Submitted: no' is treated as a human message.

* fix(email): do not restart a running mailbox on every health check

initialize() runs from the supervisor's health check and unconditionally
started a new runtime, replacing the one already polling. Its poll loop was
reset before completing a pass, so the mailbox reported connected while
never reading a single message.

A running runtime is now reused, matching the shared token controller.

* fix(email-ui): keep session titles readable in the narrow pickers

The settings dialog gives the channel column about 330px, so a per-sender
picker is ~235px wide. Options carried the full session id, making the
longest label 669px — it was clipped and the chosen session could not be
read.

Labels now show the title only, trimmed from the middle at 22 characters so
they fit, with the automation timestamp kept at the tail where it
distinguishes entries. The full id stays as the option tooltip, the rows
stack the address above a full-width picker, and a long current choice is
echoed in full beneath it.

* refactor(email): split the mailbox channel behind a transport seam

The channel talked to IMAP/SMTP directly, so supporting another mail
protocol would have meant either a second channel or protocol branches
scattered through the runtime.

The implementation now sits behind a small transport contract (connect,
disconnect, latestUid, listMessages, sendReply, sendText) in
transports/imap-smtp.mjs, while quote stripping, thread resolution, address
normalization, the allowlist, session binding, and loop prevention stay
shared in the runtime. email-api.mjs re-exports the old surface so existing
imports keep working.

Behaviour is unchanged: the full suite still passes.

* feat(email): select the mailbox transport from configuration

A mailbox now declares how it is reached, so one channel hosts every mail
protocol instead of one channel per protocol:

  imap-smtp   any standard mailbox (address + app password + server hosts)
  agent-mail  Tencent Agent Mail (address only; authorizes by QR code)

The controller builds the configured transport from an injected registry and
validates it against the contract, and bindMailbox derives its required
fields from the transport definition — an Agent mailbox has no app password
and no server hosts, so requiring them would have made it unbindable.

* feat(email): add a Tencent Agent Mail transport

The mailbox channel can now be reached over the Agent Mail protocol
(agent.qq.com) as well as IMAP/SMTP, so it stays one channel with a
transport choice rather than a second channel.

The transport implements the same six-method contract: alias resolution,
paged listings, sender filtering before any body is read, attachment
download, reply/send, and the RFC 3834 marker. It carries the protocol's
two quirks — the official CLI User-Agent the server validates, and the
CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED challenge that a send must answer — plus OAuth token
rotation, where the rotated refresh token is persisted so the next refresh
still works.

Two things the mailbox had assumed about its transport had to generalise:

- the cursor is no longer necessarily an integer. IMAP numbers messages,
  so a startup window can be stepped back; the Agent mailbox pages by an
  opaque id, so it starts at the tip. The mailbox keeps its own cursor
  instead of the shared store's integer-only one.
- the runtime no longer coerces the message id to a number.

The device flow (start + poll) is exported separately so the settings UI
can drive authorization.

* feat(email-ui): choose the mailbox transport in the connector form

The connector now leads with the access method, and the fields follow it:
IMAP/SMTP asks for a provider and an app password; the Agent mailbox asks
for neither, since it authorizes by QR code. The submit button's
requirement is derived the same way, so an Agent mailbox is not blocked on
a password it will never have.

* feat(email): carry OAuth tokens in the mailbox credential

The Agent mailbox has no app password; it holds an access/refresh token
pair. The credential already stored a JSON object under one ref (this
channel has always done that, unlike the single-secret channels), so the
pair simply joins the address there rather than needing a new store.

The refresh token rotates on every refresh, so the new pair is written
back through the controller. The shared runtime factory forwards the full
credential and a persistence callback, held in a slot because the
controller is constructed after createRuntime is defined.

* feat(email-ui): authorize the Agent mailbox by QR code

Selecting the Agent mailbox now offers an authorization step instead of a
password: it shows the authorization URL and pairing code, polls until the
server reports the authorization, and only then allows the mailbox to be
bound — the connect button stays disabled until a token pair exists.

The pending device code lives on the controller, so the flow spans two
requests (start, then poll) without the client holding protocol state.

* fix(email): name a mailbox after its address

The status payload carried the name at the top level, but the shared client
reads the identity from the `bot` object — so the name was ignored and the
settings card fell back to the generic "<channel>机器人" label, showing a
mailbox as "Email机器人".

The mailbox now reports bot.name as its address, with the masked form kept
for the secondary line. The connector form never asked for a name, so this
is purely how the account is presented.

* fix(email): honour the server's authorization window

The Agent mailbox flow hard-coded a five-minute validity window and ignored
the expires_in the server returns (600s), so the channel reported "timed
out" while the authorization was still usable, and the settings page
promised a shorter window than the real one.

The transport now reads expires_in and falls back to a value no shorter
than the server's. The controller stores the actual deadline instead of
adding a constant, and the waiting text is built from plain translatable
strings showing the real window.

The reference implementation (AtomerCore/dsh-qq-agent-mail) delegates this
whole flow to the official CLI; this keeps the self-contained version but
matches its observed timing.

* fix(email): keep a pending authorization across a reload

The device code lived only in memory, so a plugin reload lost it. The code
stays valid for ten minutes, which easily outlives a restart — the scan had
already succeeded when the server next answered "not started", and the
settings page sat on "connecting" with no way forward.

The pending code is now written through to the mailbox state, so a reloaded
controller can still redeem a completed scan; redeeming or expiring clears
it. The settings page also stops silently dropping back to idle: it clears
the stale session and surfaces the reason.

* fix(email): report the transport and let a mailbox switch it

Three gaps found while auditing the mailbox for a full sweep:

- the status payload never said which protocol a mailbox speaks, and the
  client's field list dropped it as well, so the settings page described an
  Agent mailbox with IMAP/SMTP hosts it does not have;
- updateMailboxSettings could patch hosts and the allowlist but not the
  transport, so the choice was fixed at bind time;
- the Agent transport carried a long-poll helper nothing ever called. Both
  protocols poll on the same interval, so it is removed rather than left as
  untested code.

* fix(email): reply with the transport's own message id

The Agent mailbox addresses a message by the id its API returns, not by the
RFC Message-ID header. The reply target only carried the RFC one, so the
reply path was built from an address-shaped id — an "@" that had to be
percent-encoded, or brackets stripped into the wrong value — and a reply
could miss the thread it belonged to.

The message now carries both ids and the Agent transport prefers its own,
falling back to the RFC one when a runtime does not supply it. IMAP is
unaffected: it threads by header.

* fix(email-ui): finish connecting once the authorization lands

The panel showed "authorized, connecting the mailbox…" but only stored the
tokens and waited for a second click on the bind button, so anyone who had
already scanned appeared to hang — and a page reload threw the tokens away.

A completed authorization now submits the bind itself, as soon as an address
and at least one allowed sender are present. When those are still missing the
status says so instead of implying work is underway.

* fix(email): carry the OAuth tokens into the bind

bindMailbox destructured only the password, so the token pair the scan
produced was dropped before the credential probe — the Agent mailbox was
probed with no token at all and failed with the IMAP wording ("check the
address, app password and server settings"), which pointed at the wrong
thing entirely.

The tokens are accepted, used for the probe, and persisted. A missing pair
now reports that the authorization is missing rather than that a password
is.

* fix(email): report a usable reason when a mailbox fails to start

An AggregateError carries an empty message with the reason on `code`
(ECONNREFUSED and friends). Because `??` does not fall through an empty
string, the recorded error was blank, so the settings card could say only
that something failed with no way to act on it.

The message now falls back through code, cause, and the error itself, so a
failure is diagnosable from the UI.

* fix(email): give the runtime's transport its protocol key

The runtime built the transport config without the transport key, so
createTransport always fell back to IMAP/SMTP. An Agent mailbox was then
dialled as if it were a mail server and failed with ECONNREFUSED — while the
same credentials connected fine when the transport was used directly, which
is what made the failure look like a network problem.

With the key passed through, the mailbox reaches its own API.

* fix(email): let the runtime build the configured transport

The runtime constructed its own transport and defaulted to IMAP/SMTP, so the
protocol the mailbox actually uses was ignored: an Agent mailbox was dialled
as a mail server and failed with ECONNREFUSED on port 993, even though the
same credentials connected fine through the transport directly.

The controller now injects its transport factory (the one that selects by
protocol) into the runtime, and the host factory forwards it. This is what
made the Agent mailbox unreachable while looking like a network fault.

* feat(email-ui): fill the Agent mailbox address from the authorization

The scan returns tokens, but the address is what the account is named and
bound as, and the server already knows it. Asking the user to retype it was
busywork and a chance to bind the wrong address.

The authorization now resolves the mailbox identity and returns it, so the
address field fills itself and becomes read-only in that mode, and the bind
no longer waits on a field the user cannot usefully edit. A failed lookup
does not invalidate the scan.

* test(email): cover the address field per transport

The Agent mailbox address now arrives with the authorization and the field is
read-only there, so the tests that typed it were exercising a field the user
cannot edit. They now cover the standard mode (typed address and password)
and the Agent mode (filled from the authorization) separately.

* fix(email-ui): keep the bindable session list current

The list was fetched once when the panel mounted. Sessions are created
elsewhere — chats, automations, other channels — so anything started while
the panel stayed open never appeared in the picker, and switching workspace
showed the previous workspace's sessions.

It now refreshes on a timer and on demand, so the list reflects what exists
when you look at it. The Host side was already live; only the client cached.

* fix(email-ui): refresh the per-sender rows when the allowlist changes

Saving the allowlist reloaded channel state but not the binding panel, so a
newly allowed sender was stored and simply never appeared as a row — the
value was saved and invisible.

The panel now registers its own reload with the allowlist form, so saving
refreshes the rows. The parent's reload only re-read channel state, which
is why wiring it there had no effect.

* fix(email): accept the payload shape the client actually sends

The mailbox update handler read the fields from a nested `update` object,
but the client sends them flat beside botId — as every other endpoint in the
file does. The nested read produced an empty update, so the call reported
success and changed nothing: an edited allowlist looked saved and was not.

This is why a newly allowed sender never appeared. The earlier refresh fix
was necessary but not sufficient — there was nothing new to show.

* fix(email): stop reporting a mailbox healthy once polling fails

The transport opens once and then polls forever. A poll that kept failing —
an expired token, for instance — only recorded lastError, leaving
connectionState at "connected", so the settings card showed a healthy
channel and "运行正常" while no mail could be read at all.

A failing poll now reports the mailbox as failed, and a healthy one restores
it. Opened-but-unusable is no longer presented as working.

* fix(email): never seed an opaque cursor with the newest message

The Agent mailbox lists newest-first and treats the cursor as "already
handled", so seeding it with the newest id marked that message as seen the
moment the channel connected — the first mail after connecting was never
processed, and nothing said so.

The transport's test — rather than the numeric fallback — now decides: a
numbered cursor (IMAP) still keeps the startup window, an opaque one starts
with no cursor at all. History cannot re-drive itself because the allowlist
and the seen-message set still filter.

* fix(email): read the agent mailbox body and its RFC Message-ID

The list endpoint returns only a `snippet`; the body and the RFC
Message-ID come from the per-message read. Listing alone therefore produced
a message with no text — dropped as empty — and a thread id that was really
the API's own id, which is not an RFC Message-ID and failed to parse. Mail
arrived and was silently never processed.

Bodies are now fetched after the allowlist filter, so an unlisted sender
still costs no extra request, and attachments keep their loaders.

* fix(email): de-duplicate on the message id, not only the cursor

The cursor marks a boundary in the listing, but a mailbox whose listing
shifts underneath it — mail moved, deleted, or the page the cursor lived on
no longer returned — loses that boundary. Every message then came back on
every poll, re-running a turn each time, and the newest mail looked
unprocessed because the cursor never advanced past it.

Delivery is now guarded by the seen-message set, keyed on the RFC
Message-ID, which survives a re-listing. The cursor stays as an
optimisation.

* test(email): give the seen-set test its own state file

A shared path carried seen ids between tests, so a 'fresh' message was
already recorded when the full suite ran.

* feat(email): drive the Agent mailbox with the official agently-cli

The hand-written client could not refresh its token. The server issued an
access token that worked while the matching refresh token was rejected with
`invalid_grant` the moment it was used — verified moments after a fresh
authorization, so it was not expiry — and the mailbox died about an hour
after every scan. Comparing the CLI's own request shapes across versions
found no difference to copy: the auth symbols are identical in 1.0.15 and
1.0.18, so the protocol was not the missing piece.

The official CLI keeps credentials in the system keychain, tracks
expires_at, refreshes ahead of expiry and re-authorizes a stale watcher.
That is what this transport now uses: one command per operation, JSON on
stdout, and the two-step send confirmation handled by resending with the
token. Roughly 200 lines of OAuth and refresh logic are gone, and no token
is stored by this plugin at all.

The CLI is an optional dependency: an IMAP/SMTP-only install is unaffected,
and an Agent mailbox reports a clear error when it is missing.

* fix(email): let the runtime start a mailbox that carries no token

The Agent mailbox hands the runtime an address and nothing else, because
agently-cli holds the credentials. The runtime still demanded a token, so
the mailbox reported "requires config, token, Harness, and state" and never
started.

* fix(email): isolate agent mailboxes per CLI workspace; allow later allowlists

Three repairs around the Agent mailbox:

Each mailbox authorizes in its own agently-cli workspace. The CLI separates
accounts per workspace, so sharing one meant the second Agent mailbox always
read the first account that had logged in — whichever card you authorized,
the address that came back was the first one.

AgentMailAuth referenced `address` without ever receiving it, so the
authorization button did nothing at all.

A mailbox may connect before any sender is authorized. The allowlist is what
decides who can drive it, and an empty list still admits nobody, so
connecting first and adding senders later loses no safety.

* feat(email-ui): let a bound agent mailbox re-authorize

agently-cli holds the login and it can lapse, but a bound mailbox only
offered "reconnect", which cannot renew a login — so the only way back was
to remove the mailbox and add it again.

The settings panel now offers the scan, in the mailbox's own CLI workspace,
and reloads the card once it completes.

* fix(email-ui): show the authorization link for a re-authorizing mailbox

The panel announced it had generated a link and then showed nothing, so
there was nothing to scan. The URL the server returns is now rendered, with
the pairing code, and an explicit message when it is missing.

* fix(email): fall back to the CLI default workspace

agently-cli separates accounts per workspace, but a mailbox pinned to a
workspace nobody logged into just reports "authorization required" — even
when the account that owns it is already authorized. A single authorized
account owns every Agent mailbox, so the pinned workspace is now used only
when it actually has a login, and the CLI default otherwise.

* feat(email): let a mailbox auto-approve its allowlisted senders

A request that needs a write ran only after someone replied to confirm, and
an automated message has nobody to send that reply — the answer was drafted
and the mailbox sat at replied=0.

Mail is forgeable, so this is opt-in per mailbox and off by default: when on,
the exemption follows the allowlist exactly, and a sender who is not on it
still gets no reply at all.

* fix(email): carry the approval choice through bind and status

The checkbox reads its state from the snapshot, and the field was missing in
both directions: the bind ignored it and the status never reported it, so
the form opened unchecked and disagreed with what was stored.

* fix(email): pass the agent mailbox body as an argument

`--body-file -` is not stdin: agently-cli treats the dash as a literal
filename and fails with ENOENT, so every reply and send was refused — which
surfaced as CHANNEL_DELIVERY_UNCERTAIN and left replied at zero while the
mailbox looked connected.

The text now travels with --body, and the unsupported --header flag is
dropped rather than passed through.

* chore: record the optional CLI dependency in the lockfile

package.json declared @tencent-qqmail/agently-cli but the lockfile did not
list it, so `npm ci` refused to install and CI failed before running a test.

* chore: acknowledge the email approval checkbox in package verification

The guard that limits checkable inputs counted three checkboxes, and the
email settings panel added a fourth, so verification failed after every test
had passed.

* fix(email): address the review findings

Security: the sample scripts carried a live mailbox address and app password,
and they had been committed. The credential is removed from the working tree
and from every commit that held it, and the files are ignored from here on.
The password itself still needs rotating — history cannot be unpublished.

- imap-smtp: MAX_REPLY_CHARS was used but never imported, so every send threw
  ReferenceError before reaching the network. Standard mailboxes could not
  send at all.
- agent-mail: the identity check read `platformId` while callers pass
  `address`, so it always passed; a mailbox could silently run as another
  account. It now reads either, and refuses when the address is unknown.
- agent-mail: a page is ordered oldest-first before the limit applies. Taking
  the newest N skipped the older backlog past the limit.
- agent-mail / imap-smtp: an empty allowlist means "admit nobody", not "no
  filter", so no body is fetched for mail the policy already refused.
- email-runtime: mail headers moved off `content`, which the shared layer
  parses for control commands and approval decisions; a decorated string made
  `/help` and "批准" unrecognisable. The model reads them via `controlText`'s
  sibling field instead.
- Removed the auto-approve switch. Its premise was wrong — the bridge never
  intercepts execution, so the setting changed nothing while the settings page
  claimed otherwise.

* fix(email): push the allowlist when a mailbox is bound

Direct execution for allowlisted senders is the intended behaviour, and the
policy that expresses it was only built when the settings were edited — a
freshly bound mailbox therefore admitted nobody until someone opened and
saved its settings. The policy is now applied at bind time, with a test that
pins both halves: the listed sender may execute, and nobody else may.

* fix(email): deliver mail during a parked turn, repair attachments, keep threads

Three findings from the review, each with a test:

- A turn waiting on an approval never settles, and the poll loop awaited
  `accept`, so every later message went unread until someone replied. The
  bridge already serialises per conversation, so the loop no longer waits;
  started deliveries are tracked, drained on stop, and their failures logged
  instead of surfacing as unhandled rejections.

- Agent mailbox attachments were broken in both directions. Inbound used the
  API's field names (`fileName`/`bytes`/`mediaType`) where the runtime reads
  `filename`/`size`/`contentType`, and carried no content at all — they now
  report correctly and fetch their bytes on demand. Outbound accepted only a
  path while the runtime hands over bytes, so every real attachment was
  skipped and the send still reported success; bytes are staged to a temp file
  for upload, and an attachment that can be neither read nor staged now fails
  loudly.

- The Message-ID → conversation map lived only in memory, so after a reload a
  reply on the same thread began a new session and orphaned the original. It
  is persisted with the rest of the channel state.

* fix(email): back off when the provider rate limits a poll

The Agent mailbox API answers 429 once its request budget is spent, and the
runtime retried on its fixed interval regardless — which keeps the limit
exceeded, so the mailbox never recovers on its own. A rate-limited poll now
waits, doubling the delay to a fifteen-minute ceiling and reporting retryAt,
while a successful poll resets it.

The provider publishes its limits at runtime (`+me` exposes `rate_limits`)
rather than in its documentation, so the polling interval is derived from
those numbers instead of a hard-coded value: half the declared per-minute
budget is left for reads and replies, with a floor and a fall back to the
default when the account reports none.

* fix(email): address the second review round

Five blocking findings from the review, plus a sixth found while verifying
them.

- A normal message was recorded as handled before its turn ran, so it was
  dropped silently. The seen-record now belongs to the bridge alone, and the
  poll loop keeps its own in-flight set so a re-listing cannot deliver twice.
  That set also covers the window between the bridge releasing its record and
  its queue draining. A failed turn is un-marked and retried, bounded at three
  attempts, so a transient Harness failure no longer loses the mail forever.

- Binding a fresh mailbox failed and left the config written but unusable: the
  access policy lives inside the workspace record, which only `createRuntime`
  created. `ensureWorkspace` is now extracted and injected, so the record
  exists before the policy is pushed; a failure rolls the binding back rather
  than stranding a config that points at a dead credential. A runtime that
  fails to start is deliberately NOT rolled back — it stays reconnectable.

- A backlog larger than one page was both skipped and re-downloaded. Paging now
  walks to the cursor across pages, trims at the oldest end, and reads bodies
  only for the batch it returns.

- The permission check and the approval-reply matcher read the decorated body
  (with mail headers) while execution read the plain one. `isSharedLocalCommand`
  requires a leading '/', so a prefixed '/new' never looked like a command and
  the gate never fired, while execution still ran it; a "批准" reply never
  claimed its approval. Both now use the control text, and `canExecuteCommands`
  is not used to admit any tool call.

- The email channel ships closed behind EMAIL_CHANNEL_ENABLED, as the review
  suggested: the entry point is hidden and no production controller is
  constructed, so no mailbox connects. Nothing is deleted — reopening the
  switch restores every mailbox untouched.

* chore: retrigger CI

The previous run wedged in the Run checks step: it sat in_progress for over
25 minutes with updated_at frozen two seconds after start, while the same
command completes in ~45 seconds locally and upstream runs finish in under a
minute. Nothing in the tree changed — this is an empty commit to get a fresh
runner.

* fix(email): stop wedging shutdown on an unref'd timer

`whenIdle` bounded its wait with a timer that was unref'd so shutdown could
not be held open by it. The opposite happened: an unref'd timer does not keep
the event loop alive, so when it was the only pending handle the process
finished before the timer fired and the race never resolved — `stop()` then
awaited it forever.

Locally the parked-delivery test still passed because other handles kept the
loop alive long enough for the timer to run. In CI it hung: `Run checks` sat
in_progress for over 25 minutes with no output, on two separate runners,
while the same command finishes in ~45 seconds here. The timer is now a
normal one.

CI has been failing to complete since this landed, so this is the fix rather
than a retry.

alone can be an accident, and a card would be noise.

fix(feishu): split the step card on its table count, not just its size

A single Feishu card accepts only five `table` elements. A step-streaming card
accumulates every round into one card — folded process panels included — so a
reply with three tables per round reached six on the second round and Feishu
rejected the whole update:

  230099 / ErrCode 11310 / card table number over limit

The failure is not local to that write. `#renderStepCardNow` marks the card
`broken` and stops updating it, so the client stays on the previous content and
a "running" placeholder while the answer never appears.

`splitStepStreamCardBlocks` budgeted chunks by encoded bytes only, which a card
full of short tables passes easily. It now also counts the tables a chunk would
render — in prose blocks and in folded panel lines alike — and starts a new
chunk when adding a block would exceed five. Blocks are still never dropped,
and a table is still rendered as a table rather than rewritten to plain text.

The limit and the folded-panel behaviour come from the maintainer's boundary
tests on a live bot: five tables in one card succeeded, six failed; three
folded plus two in the body succeeded, three plus three failed.

Two problems with the menu entry added for a p2p message whose body is empty
once the mention is stripped.

It did not clear the command gate. `/m` is recognised as a command, so
`canExecuteCommands: false` refuses it — but an empty body went through the
ordinary-chat path and reached `#sendMenuCard` directly. A sender who may chat
but not run commands therefore received a menu carrying workspace paths and
other session titles. Opening the menu is `/m` by another route, so it is now
treated as a command for access control and refused the same way.

The trigger was also too wide: "no text, images, files or reply" also matches a
voice note, a video, a sticker and a forwarded card, all of which lost their
own "not supported" notice and silently opened a menu instead. The condition is
narrowed to a plain `text` message in a p2p chat with nothing but the mention.

Both entry points now share `isBareMentionMenuRequest`, so the gate cannot
diverge from the route that uses it.

fix(feishu): split inside a block, and resync sealed cards after folding

Two gaps left by the first pass, both reproduced from the bridge flow.

Splitting only *between* blocks could not help when one block held too many
tables — a short answer with six small tables is a single block, so it stayed
over the limit and the card write was still rejected. A block is now broken at
table boundaries until each piece fits, and a folded panel's `lines` are
distributed the same way, since a panel's tables count toward the same card.

The render path assumed chunk boundaries were stable ("blocks only append") and
only rewrote them when the chunk *count* grew. Folding merges earlier steps into
one process panel, which redistributes the tables the splitter budgets by: the
count can stay the same while the earlier chunks' content changes. Those sealed
cards kept stale content, so a step's tables vanished from the finished card.
Sealed chunks are now re-patched whenever the split is recomputed.

fix(feishu): serialise panel syncs and stop a superseded one before it writes

Two state-consistency issues from review.

1) setSlashPanel() bumped an epoch and started a second sync while the first was
still running, and the epoch was only checked after the whole sync returned. The
older run kept deleting, waiting and creating from a plan nobody wanted anymore,
so a later save could be overwritten by the run it superseded. The runtime now
cancels the run in flight — it stops at its next checkpoint, while requests
already sent are left to finish — and queues the new one after it settles, so the
panel converges to the newest config and two plans never interleave.

2) The settings page kept showing the pre-save list: applySnapshot() cleared
`dirty`, which re-ran the snapshot effect against an account the parent never
refreshed, so the page — and the next "copy to other bots" payload — fell back to
the old panel. The saved panel now becomes the page's baseline through the same
parent-state pattern the access-policy tab already uses.

Regression tests: a superseded sync issues no further requests (registry), a save
during a running sync leaves the panel on the newest config without interleaving
(runtime), and the page keeps the saved list afterwards and copies that (client).
